claim: More than 95% of inner molecular layer interneurons with basket-like axon collaterals presented a dendritic tree that traversed nearly the entire molecular layer (174 ± 4.9 µm, n = 30 cells).
source: Two-photon laser scanning microscopy (2PLSM) of whole-cell patch-clamped inner MLIs revealed that more than 95% of cells with basket-like axon collaterals also presented a dendritic tree that traversed nearly the entire molecular layer (174 ± 4.9 µm, n = 30 cells - see Figure 1A for a representative example).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements from 2PLSM imaging of 30 cells.

claim: Extracellular stimulation of parallel fibers in the presence of gabazine produced outward currents that were detected in approximately 60% of stimulation locations across 26 cells.
source: This outward current was detected in approximately 60% of stimulation locations (Figure 1H, red bar) across 26 cells, twenty-one of which displayed significant outward currents in at least one stimulation site (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 26 cells showing detection frequency.

claim: Bath application of 10 µM NBQX eliminated both the EPSC and the subsequent outward current to below detectable levels in all tested experiments.
source: Bath application of 10 µM of the AMPA receptor (AMPAR) antagonist, NBQX, eliminated both the EPSC and the subsequent outward current to below detectable levels (Figure 1E, n = 5/5 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data from 5 experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Replacing potassium by cesium in the patch pipette solution did not affect the frequency or amplitude of outward currents.
source: To test this more directly, we replaced potassium by cesium in the patch pipette solution to block potassium conductances. We observed no difference in the frequency or amplitude of outward currents (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing K+ and Cs+ internal solutions shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: 20 µM mefloquine reduced the frequency of observing an outward current to 14.9 ± 4.4%, with detected currents being 3-fold smaller (8.7 ± 0.5 vs. 2.9 ± 0.3 pA).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, 20 µM of mefloquine, a potent blocker of gap junctions (~70% block at 20 µM [Cruikshank et al., 2004]) reduced the frequency of observing an outward current to 14.9 ± 4.4%, with those detected currents being 3-fold smaller (8.7 ± 0.5 vs. 2.9 ± 0.3 pA; Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data with mefloquine shown in Figure 1I, and cites previous work on mefloquine's blocking properties.

claim: In brain slices prepared from mature Cx36 KO mice, there was a 45% reduction in the frequency of outward currents, and the amplitude of remaining events was 3-fold smaller than age-matched recordings (4.2 ± 0.8 vs. 12.7 ± 1.8 pA).
source: In brain slices prepared from mature Cx36 KO mice, we observed a 45% reduction in the frequency of outward currents, and the amplitude of the remaining events was 3-fold smaller than age-matched recordings (4.2 ± 0.8 vs. 12.7 ± 1.8 pA).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing Cx36 KO mice to wild-type controls.

claim: One out of five BC-BC paired recordings in Cx36 KO mice exhibited bidirectional spikelets and a coupling coefficient greater than 2%.
source: We also assessed electrical coupling in BC-BC paired whole-cell recordings in Cx36 KO mice, and found that one out of five recordings exhibited bidirectional spikelets and a coupling coefficient (CC) greater than 2% (see below for criteria).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recording data from Cx36 KO mice.

claim: Nearly 60% of BC-BC pairs show detectable electrical coupling in wild-type mice.
source: This is less than the nearly 60% of BC-BC pairs showing detectable electrical coupling (see below, Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recording data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Stellar cells from older WT animals (P90-150) are 4-fold less likely to exhibit outward currents (15 vs. 79%, n = 27 and 38 stimulation sites, respectively) and exhibit 5-fold smaller outward currents (2.2 ± 0.4 vs. 12.7 ± 1.8 pA) compared to basket cells.
source: We also found that SCs from older WT animals (P90-150) are 4-fold less likely to exhibit such outward currents (15 vs. 79%, n = 27 and 38 stimulation sites, respectively) and exhibit 5-fold smaller outward currents (2.2 ± 0.4 vs. 12.7 ± 1.8 pA), consistent with the lower electrical coupling probabilities and amplitudes observed previously in P18-23 rats (Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing SCs to BCs and cites previous work in rats.

claim: Extracellular stimulation of a PF beam outside the dendritic tree of the recorded BC in the presence of gabazine produced rapid and small inward currents invariably observed prior to large relative outward currents in all tested locations.
source: Indeed, rapid and small inward currents were invariably observed prior to large relative outward currents (see example cell in Figure 3A–E; n = 11/11 stimulation locations from 9 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 11 stimulation locations across 9 cells shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: Both inward and outward current components increased with increasing extracellular stimulus intensity, consistent with recruitment of at least one electrically coupled MLI.
source: Both current components increased with increasing extracellular stimulus intensity (from 20 to 50 V), consistent with recruitment of at least one electrically coupled MLI (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stimulus intensity-dependent responses in Figure 3E.

claim: Direct stimulation of neighboring MLIs in the presence of 10 µM NBQX revealed that each time an outward current was detected, it was preceded by a detectable inward current (n = 17/17 stimulation sites from 13 cells).
source: When looking at the mean of all responses for each stimulation intensity, we found that each time an outward current was detected, it was preceded by a detectable inward current (n = 17/17 stimulation sites from 13 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 17 stimulation sites across 13 cells.

claim: Gabazine did not affect coupling coefficients between basket cells.
source: Summary plot of unidirectional coupling coefficients (CCs), showing that they are not significantly altered by gabazine addition (n = 16 cells from 8 BC pairs, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p=0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of paired recording data from 8 BC pairs shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The amplitudes of the inward and outward currents (or their corresponding synaptic potentials) correlated with the bidirectional coupling coefficients for each cell pair.
source: Indeed, the amplitudes of the inward and outward currents (or their corresponding synaptic potentials) correlated with the bidirectional CCs for each cell pair (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Spikelets could generally be detected if the coupling coefficients were greater than 2%.
source: Given the number of trials (n = 30 sweeps), spikelets could generally be detected if the CCs were greater than 2% (see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of detection thresholds shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The peak amplitude of the inward and outward currents, as well as the charge transfer of the spikelet response, were unaffected by altering the holding potential of the receiving neuron (n = 12 cells from six pairs).
source: The peak amplitude of the inward and outward currents, as well as the charge transfer of the spikelet response, were unaffected by altering the holding potential of the receiving neuron (Figure 5B, n = 12 cells from six pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells across 6 pairs shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When adjusting the holding current to alter the membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron between approximately −80, –70 or −60 mV, the inward current component of the spikelet reduced in amplitude and the outward current component increased (n = 12 cells from six pairs).
source: In contrast, when adjusting the holding current to alter the membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron between approximately −80, –70 or −60 mV, the inward current component of the spikelet reduced in amplitude and the outward current component increased (Figure 5D; n = 12 cells from six pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells across 6 pairs shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The compound effect of inward and outward current changes led to an inversion of charge transfer from net excitation to net inhibition as the presynaptic neuron was depolarized.
source: Because of the slower outward component, the compound effect of inward and outward current changes led to an inversion of charge transfer from net excitation to net inhibition as the presynaptic neuron was depolarized.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of changes in inward and outward currents with presynaptic membrane potential.

claim: The slopes of the regression lines from the three presynaptic membrane potential groups (−60, –70 and −80 mV) were significantly different (F-test, p-value=0.0003), indicating that the ratio of inward and outward currents is a reliable indicator of presynaptic resting membrane potential.
source: In paired recordings, the slopes of the regression lines from the three presynaptic membrane potential groups (−60,–70 and −80 mV) were significantly different (F-test, p-value=0.0003), indicating that the ratio of inward and outward currents is a reliable indicator of presynaptic resting membrane potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of regression lines from paired recordings.

claim: The regression line of the off-beam stimulation group was comparable to the −60 mV group from paired recordings (p-value=0.93).
source: The regression line of the off-beam stimulation group was comparable to the −60 mV group from paired recordings (p-value=0.93), but the linear relationship was significantly different from the direct stimulation group and the −60 mV group (p-value=0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of regression lines.

claim: MLIs in brain slices have a depolarized resting membrane potential, greater than −60 mV.
source: Provided that the voltage-dependence of the shape of the presynaptic AP is similar between patch-dialyzed and unperturbed cells, these data indicate that MLIs in brain slices have a depolarized resting membrane potential, greater than −60 mV (i.e. more depolarized).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of spikelet waveforms between paired recordings and extracellular stimulation.

claim: The depolarized membrane potential amplifies the AHP in the presynaptic neuron and ensures that spikelets deliver a net inhibition.
source: This depolarized membrane potential amplifies the AHP in the presynaptic neuron and ensures that spikelets deliver a net inhibition, which provides another mechanism of FFI within the MLI network, in addition to chemical transmission.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of spikelet polarity dependence on presynaptic membrane potential.

claim: Bidirectional spikelet transmission was significantly more likely to be observed than unidirectional GABAergic connections (58 ± 6%, n = 35/60 paired recordings, and 41 ± 5%, n = 35/85 connections, respectively; p=0.04).
source: We found that bidirectional spikelet transmission was significantly more likely to be observed than unidirectional GABAergic connections, (58 ± 6%, n = 35/60 paired recordings, and 41 ± 5%, n = 35/85 connections, respectively; p=0.04, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of paired recording data comparing electrical and chemical connections.

claim: In 15 of 28 unidirectional connections from BC-BC pairs, the GABAAR antagonist gabazine did not alter the outward current amplitude.
source: If we analyzed the gabazine experiments only, we found that in 15 of 28 unidirectional connections from BC-BC pairs, the GABAAR antagonist did not alter the outward current amplitude, consistent with a larger fraction of electrical than chemical connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data from 28 connections.

claim: In the remaining connections where gabazine was tested, the fractional block by 10 μM gabazine was ~50% on average.
source: In the remaining connections the fractional block by 10 μM gabazine was ~50% on average (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that, when both chemical and electrical synapses were present, the outward current under our recording conditions was similar.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For cases where increasing stimulation intensity elicited a detectable outward current, the half-width in current-clamp conditions was decreased by 21 ± 4% (n = 9, p=0.004).
source: For the cases where additional stimulation intensity elicited a detectable outward current, the half-width in current-clamp conditions was decreased by 21 ± 4% (n = 9, p=0.004; Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 9 stimulation sites shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Temporal summation of EPSPs in response to five stimuli at 50 Hz was significantly reduced at stimulus locations that recruited spikelets (n = 27 stimulation sites in the 'no spikelet' group versus n = 22 stimulation sites in the 'spikelet' group; p=0.004).
source: Temporal summation of EPSPs in response to five stimuli at 50 Hz was significantly reduced at stimulus locations that recruited spikelets (Figure 7F; n = 27 stimulation sites in the 'no spikelet' group versus n = 22 stimulation sites in the 'spikelet' group; p=0.004, Two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of temporal summation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Coincident stimulation of spikelets and EPSPs increased the EPSP peak amplitude (averaged over a 4–6 ms window) by 21.3 ± 2.4% (n = 12, p<0.0001).
source: Coincident stimulation of spikelets and EPSPs indeed increased the EPSP peak amplitude (averaged over a 4–6 ms window) by 21.3 ± 2.4% (n = 12, p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test - Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells shown in Figure 8E.

claim: If spikelet recruitment preceded the EPSP (by 5 to 75 ms), the peak amplitude of the EPSP was significantly reduced, with a maximal reduction of 20 ± 2.9% at Δt = 20 ms (n = 12, p<0.0001).
source: However, if spikelet recruitment preceded the EPSP (by 5 to 75 ms), the peak amplitude of the EPSP was significantly reduced, with a maximal reduction of 20 ± 2.9% at Δt = 20 ms (n = 12, p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs; Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Spikelets concomitant with EPSPs reduced their half-width by 16.7 ± 1.8%.
source: We also confirmed that spikelets concomitant with EPSPs reduced their half-width by 16.7 ± 1.8%, consistent with results described above in Figure 7D.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data consistent with previous findings.

claim: The relative spike probability was increased by 49.3 ± 8% for coincidental arrival of both inputs, and decreased by 40.5 ± 6.1% if EPSPs were triggered 20 ms after the spikelets (p-values<0.001; n = 11 cells for both).
source: We found that the relative spike probability was increased by 49.3 ± 8% for coincidental arrival of both inputs, and decreased by 40.5 ± 6.1% if EPSPs were triggered 20 ms after the spikelets (p-values<0.001; n = 11 cells for both; Wilcoxon matched-pairs; Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 11 cells shown in Figure 8G.

claim: MLIs within the cerebellar cortex have been shown to provide feed-forward inhibition onto Purkinje cells in vitro.
source: MLIs within the cerebellar cortex have been shown to provide FFI onto PCs in vitro (Dizon and Khodakhah, 2011; Mittmann et al., 2005; Valera et al., 2016) and in vivo (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MLIs of the cerebellar cortex are known to communicate through both chemical and electrical synapses.
source: MLIs of the cerebellar cortex are known to communicate through both chemical and electrical synapses (Kondo and Marty, 1998; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABAergic chemical synapses provide self-inhibition between MLIs.
source: GABAergic chemical synapses provide self-inhibition between MLIs (Mittmann et al., 2005), and have been suggested to mediate disinhibition of PCs (Blot et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical synapses between molecular layer interneurons within the cerebellum have been shown to mediate synchronized firing.
source: Electrical synapses between molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) within the cerebellum have been shown to mediate synchronized firing (Gaffield and Christie, 2017; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999) and sequence detection (Alcami, 2018), while those between Golgi cells have been shown to either synchronize or desynchronize cerebellar cortical network activity (Dugué et al., 2009; van Welie et al., 2016; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The presence of electrical synapses has been shown to modulate passive properties in interneurons.
source: Finally, the presence of electrical synapses has been shown to modulate passive properties in interneurons (Alcami, 2018; Amsalem et al., 2016; Hjorth et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Basket cells have been shown to precisely control the timing of Purkinje cell activity with millisecond precision.
source: Specifically, basket cells (BCs) have been shown to precisely control the timing of PC activity with millisecond precision (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MLIs in young animals have been shown to be electrically coupled via the gap junction protein Cx36, likely located in the dendrites.
source: MLIs in young animals have also been shown to be electrically coupled via the gap junction protein Cx36, likely located in the dendrites (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There is an increasing spatial gradient of occurrence and strength of electrical connectivity between MLIs from increasing depths in molecular layer.
source: It has been shown that there is an increasing spatial gradient of occurrence and strength of electrical connectivity between MLIs from increasing depths in molecular layer (Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MLIs located in the deepest (inner) third of the molecular layer are likely to be basket cells.
source: Since MLIs located in the deepest (inner) third of the molecular layer are likely to be BCs (Sultan and Bower, 1998), we investigated if electrical transmission could be recruited in a feed-forward (FF) manner in the BC population, and how it modulates EPSP-spike coupling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Spikelet transmission through electrical synapses has been shown to exhibit a long-lasting inhibitory current.
source: Spikelet transmission through electrical synapses has been shown to exhibit a long-lasting inhibitory current (Alcami and Marty, 2013; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mefloquine is a potent blocker of gap junctions with approximately 70% block at 20 µM.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, 20 µM of mefloquine, a potent blocker of gap junctions (~70% block at 20 µM [Cruikshank et al., 2004]) reduced the frequency of observing an outward current to 14.9 ± 4.4%, with those detected currents being 3-fold smaller (8.7 ± 0.5 vs. 2.9 ± 0.3 pA; Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing mefloquine's blocking properties.

claim: Previous reports showed complete block of electrical coupling at P10-13 in Cx36 KO mice.
source: The remaining electrical coupling could be due to a late-onset (3–5 months) partial compensatory mechanism, in contrast to previous reports that showed complete block at P10-13 (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The relative contribution of the depolarizing component or the after-hyperpolarization component of the presynaptic AP to the spikelet waveform can vary across cell types and determines if electrical synapses mediate net excitation or inhibition.
source: The relative contribution of the depolarizing component (Hu and Agmon, 2015; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999) or the after-hyperpolarization component (Dugué et al., 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010) of the presynaptic AP to the spikelet waveform can vary across cell types and determines if electrical synapses mediate net excitation or inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Alterations in the spikelet waveform can arise from alterations in presynaptic AP shape, which can be modulated by variations in the membrane potential of unperturbed neurons when they are not spiking (resting membrane potential).
source: Alterations in the spikelet waveform can arise from alterations in presynaptic AP shape, which can be modulated by variations in the membrane potential of unperturbed neurons when they are not spiking (resting membrane potential) (Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2013; Russo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theoretical studies show that net depolarizing spikelets will drive synchronization within neuronal networks, while hyperpolarizing spikelets will generate bistable networks which either oscillate synchronously or remain in asynchronous states.
source: Theoretical studies show that net depolarizing spikelets will drive synchronization within neuronal networks, while hyperpolarizing spikelets will generate bistable networks which either oscillate synchronously or remain in asynchronous states (Ostojic et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Coherent firing of MLIs is required for encoding precise movement kinematics.
source: Coherent firing of MLIs is required for encoding precise movement kinematics (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Whisker movement kinematics can be both encoded and driven by precise PC firing patterns.
source: Whisker movement kinematics can be both encoded (Chen et al., 2016) and driven by precise PC firing patterns (Bosman et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Synchronized PC activity can precisely gate deep cerebellar nuclear neurons to drive movement.
source: Synchronized PC activity can then precisely gate deep cerebellar nuclear neurons (Özcan et al., 2020; Person and Raman, 2012) to drive movement (Brown and Raman, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vivo evidence shows that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale.
source: Finally, in vivo evidence that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale supports their important role in timing cerebellar cortical output (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Feed-forward inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit.
source: These different computational functions are classified according to canonical wiring motifs (Feldmeyer et al., 2018; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011): feed-back inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit, while feed-forward (FF) inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling (Blot et al., 2016; Mittmann et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Feed-forward inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling.
source: These different computational functions are classified according to canonical wiring motifs (Feldmeyer et al., 2018; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011): feed-back inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit, while feed-forward (FF) inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling (Blot et al., 2016; Mittmann et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Feed-forward motifs can expand the dynamic range of inputs which can be represented by principal cells.
source: FF motifs can also expand the dynamic range of inputs which can be represented by principal cells (Pouille et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Electrical synapses between neurons are thought to generate emergent properties such as oscillations and synchronized firing within neuronal assemblies.
source: While chemical synapses can regulate interneuron firing in the same way as for principal neurons (Mittmann et al., 2005), the presence of gap junctions that couple neurons directly as resistive elements are thought to generate emergent properties such as oscillations and synchronized firing within neuronal assemblies (Beierlein et al., 2000; Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Draguhn et al., 1998; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Maex and De Schutter, 2007; Ostojic et al., 2009; van Welie et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Theoretical studies show the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within feed-forward circuits.
source: However, despite theoretical studies showing the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within FF circuits (Pham and Haas, 2019), experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within FF neural circuits has not been demonstrated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within feed-forward neural circuits has not been demonstrated prior to this study.
source: However, despite theoretical studies showing the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within FF circuits (Pham and Haas, 2019), experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within FF neural circuits has not been demonstrated.
evidence: The claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Spikelet waveforms have been shown to depend on a variety of physiological parameters across different cell types, including resting membrane potential and active conductances in the presynaptic or the postsynaptic cell.
source: Spikelet waveforms have been shown to depend on a variety of physiological parameters across different cell types, including resting membrane potential (Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2013) and active conductances in the presynaptic (Curti and Pereda, 2004; Pereda et al., 2013; Russo et al., 2013) or the postsynaptic cell (Dugué et al., 2009; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Previous recordings showing mostly depolarizing spikelets in cerebellar MLIs were due to either hyperpolarized holding potentials or an intrinsic difference in the amplitude of the AHP recorded from brain slices prepared from P11-13 rats.
source: We postulate that previous recordings showing mostly depolarizing spikelets in cerebellar MLIs were due to either hyperpolarized holding potentials (Alcami, 2018) or an intrinsic difference in the amplitude of the AHP recorded from brain slices prepared from P11-13 rats.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors to explain differences with previous studies.

claim: The resting membrane potential of MLIs is close to threshold.
source: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by three factors: (1) overlap of MLI dendritic trees in order to more likely receive common synaptic input (see Figure 6A), (2) a resting membrane potential close to threshold (Figure 5E; Kim et al., 2014), and (3) a strong enough CC, sufficient to transmit detectable spikelets (>2.3%; Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5E and citation to a previous study.

claim: The mean coupling coefficient between basket cells was 9.5%, similar to the 12% found in Golgi cells.
source: The mean CC was 9.5%, similar to the 12% found in Golgi cells (Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to a previous study.

claim: There is no correlation in coupling coefficient over intersomatic distances up to 60 µm.
source: In support of the sagittal propagation of spikelets, we find no correlation in CC over intersomatic distances up to 60 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In vitro experiments revealed that electrical connectivity in the MLI population increases convergence from MLIs to PCs.
source: Moreover, in vitro experiments revealed that electrical connectivity in the MLI population increases convergence from MLIs to PCs (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The lateral spread of PF EPSPs through electrical synapses would contribute to increasing the effective convergence between MLI and PC.
source: Finally, the lateral spread of PF EPSPs through electrical synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as previously observed in Golgi cells (Vervaeke et al., 2012), along with spikelet transmission, would also contribute to increasing the effective convergence between MLI and PC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations and comparison to previous findings.

claim: A biphasic correlogram in vivo suggested an initial excitation of PCs followed by a brief (8 ms) inhibition of PC firing.
source: In one of the few studies examining the activity of BCs and PCs in vivo (Blot et al., 2016), a biphasic correlogram suggested an initial excitation of PCs followed by a brief (8 ms) inhibition of PC firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent double-patch recordings in vivo show that even a single deep MLI (likely BC) can drive detectable inhibition of PC firing.
source: Recent double-patch recordings in vivo show that even a single deep MLI (likely BC) can drive detectable inhibition of PC firing (Arlt and Häusser, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad.
source: Interestingly, voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad (Chu et al., 2012), consistent with the presence of electrical synapses, and perhaps explaining the predominant inhibition of PC firing in response to sensory stimuli (Bosman et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Millisecond inhibition of PC firing by sensory stimuli can disinhibit cerebellar nuclei, which in turn drive motor responses.
source: Finally, in vivo evidence that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale supports their important role in timing cerebellar cortical output (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016). We therefore propose that eFFM could be an important mechanism to achieve robust, globally synchronous and precisely timed control of PC firing that in turn can efficiently drive cerebellar output from the deep nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: Experiments were performed on acute brain slices prepared from postnatal day 30–60 (~44 days on average) WT CB6F1 mice.
source: Experiments were performed on acute brain slices prepared from postnatal day 30–60 (~44 days on average) WT CB6F1 mice, which were bred in house from a cross between female BALB/cByJ and male C57BL/6J obtained from Charles River Laboratories.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: All experiments were performed on both female and male mice without bias.
source: All experiments were performed on both female and male mice without bias.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Series resistance was 14.0 ± 5.8 (mean ± SD, estimated from n = 160 cells) and always under 30 MΩ.
source: Series resistance was 14.0 ± 5.8 (mean ± SD, estimated from n = 160 cells) and always under 30 MΩ.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental recording conditions.

claim: Liquid junction potential was estimated to be −8 mV for K+-based internal solution and −11 mV for Cs+-based internal solutions.
source: All values of membrane potential were corrected for liquid junction potential, estimated to be −8 mV for K+-based internal solution and −11 mV for Cs+-based internal solutions (Figure 1; Abrahamsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and cites a previous study for the estimation method.

claim: 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs.
source: We observed that 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 (nearly 80% of locations in P90-150 animals – Figure 2) produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs, and thus generate a spikelet in the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from different age groups.

claim: Nearly 80% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P90-150 produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs.
source: We observed that 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 (nearly 80% of locations in P90-150 animals – Figure 2) produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs, and thus generate a spikelet in the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from older animals shown in Figure 2.

claim: This high degree of electrical connectivity can provide a global network mechanism spanning >100 µm in the sagittal plane for generating a feed-forward modulation of PC spiking patterns through synchronous inhibition.
source: This high degree of electrical connectivity can provide a global network mechanism spanning >100 µm in the sagittal plane (Rieubland et al., 2014) for generating a FF modulation of PC spiking patterns through synchronous inhibition (i.e., excitation of MLIs) followed by a rapid disinhibition (i.e., MLI self-inhibition).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings and cites previous work on spatial extent.

claim: Electrical feed-forward modulation could ensure an enhanced and brief BC network recruitment necessary for precise refinement of PC firing patterns.
source: Thus, eFFM could ensure an enhanced and brief BC network recruitment necessary for precise refinement of PC firing patterns.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Electrical synapses between BCs could provide a network-amplified, highly synchronous inhibition onto PCs along the parasagittal plane, despite complex spatio-temporal activation patterns of PFs.
source: Electrical synapses between BCs could provide a network-amplified, highly synchronous inhibition onto PCs along the parasagittal plane, despite complex spatio-temporal activation patterns of PFs.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Electrical feed-forward modulation could be an important mechanism to achieve robust, globally synchronous and precisely timed control of PC firing that in turn can efficiently drive cerebellar output from the deep nuclei.
source: We therefore propose that eFFM could be an important mechanism to achieve robust, globally synchronous and precisely timed control of PC firing that in turn can efficiently drive cerebellar output from the deep nuclei.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: Spikelet transmission can propagate within the BC network to generate synchronous inhibition of Purkinje cells, which can entrain cerebellar output for driving temporally precise behaviors.
source: Therefore, spikelet transmission can propagate within the BC network to generate synchronous inhibition of Purkinje cells, which can entrain cerebellar output for driving temporally precise behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Classical excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) are followed by GABAA receptor-independent outward currents, reflecting the hyperpolarization component of spikelets.
source: By combining whole-cell patch-clamp and 2-photon laser scanning microscopy of basket cells (BCs), we found that classical excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) are followed by GABAA receptor-independent outward currents, reflecting the hyperpolarization component of spikelets (a synapse-evoked action potential passively propagating from electrically coupled neighbors).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental findings described in the abstract.

claim: Feed-forward recruitment of the spikelet-mediated inhibition curtails the integration time window of concomitant excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and dampens their temporal integration.
source: FF recruitment of the spikelet-mediated inhibition curtails the integration time window of concomitant excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and dampens their temporal integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental findings described in the abstract.

claim: In contrast with GABAergic-mediated feed-forward inhibition, the depolarizing component of spikelets transiently increases the peak amplitude of EPSPs, and thus postsynaptic spiking probability.
source: In contrast with GABAergic-mediated feed-forward inhibition, the depolarizing component of spikelets transiently increases the peak amplitude of EPSPs, and thus postsynaptic spiking probability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental findings described in the abstract.

claim: The outward current peak amplitude is independent of the distance from stimulation site to the soma.
source: Outward currents were also detected all along the dendritic tree, with an amplitude independent of the distance from stimulation site to the soma (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Single-sweep analysis within each stimulus condition did not reveal any correlation between EPSC and outward current peak amplitudes.
source: In the absence of NBQX, increasing the stimulation voltage increased the amplitude of both the inward and outward currents, but single-sweep analysis within each stimulus condition did not reveal any correlation between their peak amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), despite quantal variability in the peak EPSC.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: This finding is not consistent with voltage-dependent potassium conductance recruitment by unclamped synaptic currents in dendrites for larger synaptic currents.
source: This finding is not consistent with voltage-dependent potassium conductance recruitment by unclamped synaptic currents in dendrites for larger synaptic currents (Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and cites a previous study for comparison.

claim: In conditions where only 0.1% DMSO was added to the ACSF, neither the frequency nor the amplitude of the outward current differed from control.
source: In conditions where only 0.1% DMSO was added to the artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF), neither the frequency nor the amplitude of the outward current differed from control (Figure 1H and I, pink group).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: The remaining electrical coupling in Cx36 KO mice could be due to a late-onset (3–5 months) partial compensatory mechanism.
source: The remaining electrical coupling could be due to a late-onset (3–5 months) partial compensatory mechanism, in contrast to previous reports that showed complete block at P10-13 (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors to explain the experimental findings.

claim: These alterations in electrical coupling, either using acute block of gap junctions or via Cx36 knockdown, point to gap junctions as the mechanism for generating synapse-evoked outward currents.
source: These alterations in electrical coupling, either using acute block of gap junctions or via Cx36 knockdown, point to gap junctions as the mechanism for generating synapse-evoked outward currents.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental manipulations.

claim: This manipulation sometimes allowed the isolation of putative subthreshold EPSCs propagating from the presynaptic electrical neighbor at intermediate stimulus intensities (in 2/11 stimulation locations).
source: We also note that this manipulation sometimes allowed the isolation of putative subthreshold EPSCs propagating from the presynaptic electrical neighbor at intermediate stimulus intensities (in 2/11 stimulation locations; see example in Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that spikelet-like responses recorded in this configuration could be a mixture of pure spikelets and EPSCs filtered across electrical synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spikelet-like responses recorded in off-beam configuration could be a mixture of pure spikelets and EPSCs filtered across electrical synapses.
source: We also note that this manipulation sometimes allowed the isolation of putative subthreshold EPSCs propagating from the presynaptic electrical neighbor at intermediate stimulus intensities (in 2/11 stimulation locations; see example in Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that spikelet-like responses recorded in this configuration could be a mixture of pure spikelets and EPSCs filtered across electrical synapses.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The increasing size of both the inward and outward synapse-evoked components were presumably due to the recruitment of additional electrically coupled cells.
source: The increasing size of both the inward and outward synapse-evoked components were presumably due to the recruitment of additional electrically coupled cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: For small CCs between 2% and 5%, spikelets were not always observed, which could be explained by an electrical connection via an intermediate third MLI.
source: However, for small CCs between 2% and 5% we did not always observe a spikelet (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which could be explained by an electrical connection via an intermediate third MLI (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a speculation to explain the experimental observations and cites a previous study.

claim: These results argue strongly that spikelet transmission is mediated by the same gap junctions that generate electrical coupling.
source: These results argue strongly that spikelet transmission is mediated by the same gap junctions that generate electrical coupling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The ratio of inward and outward current peak amplitudes can be used to estimate the resting membrane potential of electrically coupled cells without the need for direct whole-cell recording.
source: These results reveal the critical importance of presynaptic membrane potential on the net polarity of spikelets, and suggest that the ratio of inward/outward current peak amplitudes can be used to estimate the resting membrane potential of electrically coupled cells without the need for direct whole-cell recording.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The difference between the off-beam-elicited and directly evoked spikelets could be due to the passage of subthreshold EPSCs transmitted from presynaptic neurons in the off-beam synaptic stimulation case.
source: The difference between the off-beam-elicited and directly evoked spikelets could be due to the passage of subthreshold EPSCs transmitted from presynaptic neurons in the off-beam synaptic stimulation case, which contributes an additional inward current (See Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and an underestimation of the relative outward current.
evidence: The claim is a speculation to explain the experimental observations.

claim: We cannot rule out the possibility that GABAergic transmission is more sensitive to rundown and might bias the estimate of the relative contribution of electrical and chemical synapses.
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that GABAergic transmission is more sensitive to rundown and might bias the estimate of the relative contribution of electrical and chemical synapses.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Our data suggest that, in adult animals, electrical synapses between BCs are more likely to mediate FFI than their chemical counterparts.
source: Nevertheless, our data suggest that, in adult animals, electrical synapses between BCs are more likely to mediate FFI than their chemical counterparts.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The variability in the EPSC decay across stimulation locations in response to low-intensity stimulation could be due to the variability in cable filtering when eliciting synapse stimulation in different locations within the dendrite, or the variability in the number of electrically coupled cells.
source: The variability in the EPSC decay across stimulation locations in response to low-intensity stimulation could be due to the variability in cable filtering when eliciting synapse stimulation in different locations within the dendrite, or the variability in the number of electrically coupled cells, which have been shown to decrease input resistance (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculation to explain the experimental observations and cites a previous study.

claim: A small spikelet may accelerate some EPSPs without eliciting a detectable outward current.
source: But we cannot rule out that a small spikelet may accelerate some EPSPs without eliciting a detectable outward current.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Recruiting an additional spikelet, on average, accelerated EPSP decays.
source: Nevertheless, recruiting an additional spikelet, on average, accelerated EPSP decays.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: These results support the notion that FF recruitment of spikelets sharpens the temporal precision of EPSPs, as is the case for classical, chemical FFI.
source: These results support the notion that FF recruitment of spikelets sharpens the temporal precision of EPSPs, as is the case for classical, chemical FFI.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A unique property of spikelet-mediated FF modulation is the ability to enhance spike probability during brief time windows and decrease it for longer ones, a form of temporal contrast enhancement.
source: Thus, a unique property of spikelet-mediated FF modulation is the ability to enhance spike probability during brief time windows and decrease it for longer ones, a form of temporal contrast enhancement of information conveyed by spatially clustered axonal beams (Wilms and Häusser, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and cites a previous study.

claim: For independent PF beams, the MLI network can detect coincident excitation that will in turn generate a global and precise inhibition of downstream PCs.
source: Moreover, for independent PF beams, the MLI network can detect coincident excitation that will in turn generate a global and precise inhibition of downstream PCs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Synapse-evoked spikelet recruitment in a FF motif can act as a mechanism for temporal contrast enhancement of information flow within neural circuits.
source: Thus, synapse-evoked spikelet recruitment in a FF motif can act as a mechanism for temporal contrast enhancement of information flow within neural circuits.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: We propose that eFFI is mostly provided by other BCs because of the low frequency (13%) of BC-SC electrical coupling.
source: Because of the low frequency (13%) of BC-SC electrical coupling (Rieubland et al., 2014), we propose that eFFI is mostly provided by other BCs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and cites a previous study.

claim: The degree of temporal contrast enhancement could be enhanced by cFFI or regulated by factors that adjust presynaptic spike shape, in particular the relative size of the AHP.
source: The degree of such temporal contrast enhancement could be enhanced by cFFI or regulated by factors that adjust presynaptic spike shape, in particular the relative size of the AHP, and thus regulate the temporal balance of excitation and inhibition.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Despite the net inhibitory drive of BC spikelets, they also show a prominent brief inward (depolarizing) current component.
source: We observed that despite the net inhibitory drive of BC spikelets, they also show a prominent brief inward (depolarizing) current component.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The depolarizing component of the spikelet effectively provides FF excitation and is thus capable of synchronizing electrically coupled interneurons.
source: This depolarizing component of the spikelet effectively provides FF excitation and is thus capable of synchronizing electrically coupled interneurons (Alcami, 2018; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999), whereas the hyperpolarization component could generate low-frequency resonance in a resting state of the network (Dugué et al., 2009) and/or desynchronize network activity upon synaptic stimulation (Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings and cites previous studies.

claim: The hyperpolarization component could generate low-frequency resonance in a resting state of the network and/or desynchronize network activity upon synaptic stimulation.
source: This depolarizing component of the spikelet effectively provides FF excitation and is thus capable of synchronizing electrically coupled interneurons (Alcami, 2018; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999), whereas the hyperpolarization component could generate low-frequency resonance in a resting state of the network (Dugué et al., 2009) and/or desynchronize network activity upon synaptic stimulation (Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on previous studies.

claim: BCs are more likely to transmit spikelets than chemical inhibition to their neighbors, which could account for the narrowed excitatory responses of BCs versus SCs in vivo.
source: Nevertheless, we found that BCs are more likely to transmit spikelets than chemical inhibition to their neighbors (58 versus 41%, Figure 6), which could account for the narrowed excitatory responses of BCs versus SCs in vivo (Chu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings and cites a previous study.

claim: BC spikes have a stronger influence on PC spiking than SCs.
source: Recent in vivo findings show that BC spikes have a stronger influence on PC spiking than SCs (Arlt and Häusser, 2020), implying that the specific timing of BCs will strongly influence PC output.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The specific timing of BCs will strongly influence PC output.
source: Recent in vivo findings show that BC spikes have a stronger influence on PC spiking than SCs (Arlt and Häusser, 2020), implying that the specific timing of BCs will strongly influence PC output.
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous findings.

claim: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by overlap of MLI dendritic trees in order to more likely receive common synaptic input.
source: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by three factors: (1) overlap of MLI dendritic trees in order to more likely receive common synaptic input (see Figure 6A), (2) a resting membrane potential close to threshold (Figure 5E; Kim et al., 2014), and (3) a strong enough CC, sufficient to transmit detectable spikelets (>2.3%; Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by a strong enough CC, sufficient to transmit detectable spikelets (>2.3%).
source: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by three factors: (1) overlap of MLI dendritic trees in order to more likely receive common synaptic input (see Figure 6A), (2) a resting membrane potential close to threshold (Figure 5E; Kim et al., 2014), and (3) a strong enough CC, sufficient to transmit detectable spikelets (>2.3%; Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: This very narrow and powerful inhibition could indeed be the result of precisely synchronized BC activity followed by self-inhibition, both mediated by eFFM.
source: This very narrow and powerful inhibition could indeed be the result of precisely synchronized BC activity followed by self-inhibition, both mediated by eFFM.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: Such a network-wide synchronization would be less efficient via chemical inhibition, which has no depolarizing component and would be more variable from trial to trial due to the quantal properties of chemical transmission.
source: Such a network-wide synchronization would be less efficient via chemical inhibition, which has no depolarizing component and would be more variable from trial to trial due to the quantal properties of chemical transmission.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on known properties of chemical transmission.

claim: BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad, consistent with the presence of electrical synapses.
source: Interestingly, voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad (Chu et al., 2012), consistent with the presence of electrical synapses, and perhaps explaining the predominant inhibition of PC firing in response to sensory stimuli (Bosman et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous findings and the current experimental results.

source: Interestingly, voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad (Chu et al., 2012), consistent with the presence of electrical synapses, and perhaps explaining the predominant inhibition of PC firing in response to sensory stimuli (Bosman et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016).
